title: A Safe Implementation Plan

production_notes: No facts to verify (content.md Review Flags: None). The implementation plan is a hypothetical illustration; no real figures or rules are stated.
Dr. Ayesha Siddiqui (Pakistan) and the tuberculosis X-ray tool are hypothetical. A clinician reads every X-ray and the tool never clears one alone; keep on-screen text consistent.
Last lesson of the course: the CTA congratulates learners and points to the capstone submission. Show the submission checklist from capstone_rubric.md on the closing slide.
Stock footage must show no readable patient information or real hospital names.

Hook.voiceover: A tool that passed every test can still fail on its first Monday in a real clinic. A safe implementation plan assumes this can happen, finds problems early, and knows in advance when to stop.

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, you built your risk table. Now comes capstone step three, the implementation plan. A safe plan has seven parts. The first is silent-mode testing. The tool runs on real, current cases, but clinicians do not see its outputs, and care continues as usual. The team compares outputs with what actually happened, including by patient group.

slide.title: Seven parts of a safe plan
slide.body: Timeline of seven steps. Step 1 lit: Silent mode (tool runs, outputs hidden, care as usual, compare by patient group).

Explain.voiceover: The second part is a small pilot in one ward, clinic or team, for a fixed period, with extra support. The third is staff training on what the tool is for, what it is not for, its weaknesses, automation bias, and how to report problems. The fourth is a governance group that owns the tool, and decides whether to continue, change or stop.

slide.title: Seven parts of a safe plan
slide.body: Steps 2 to 4 lit: Small pilot (one ward, fixed period) · Staff training (purpose, limits, automation bias, reporting) · Governance group (clinical, nursing, quality, IT, data protection, patients).

Explain.voiceover: The fifth part is monitoring. Decide in advance what you measure. Include performance, equity, meaning the same measures by patient group and site, use, such as how often outputs are overridden, and the clinical value outcome from your capstone. The sixth is feedback, an easy way for staff and patients to report problems.

slide.title: Seven parts of a safe plan
slide.body: Steps 5 and 6 lit: Monitoring (performance · equity by group and site · use and overrides · outcomes) · Feedback channels (simple form or named contact, linked to incident reporting).

Explain.voiceover: The seventh part is stop criteria and a withdrawal plan. Before launch, write down what would make you pause or stop, such as performance falling in any patient group, a serious incident, or a data feed failure. And plan how care returns safely to the previous process.

slide.title: Seven parts of a safe plan
slide.body: Step 7 lit with a stop sign: Stop criteria (performance drop in any group · serious incident · data feed failure) + Withdrawal plan (who decides, how staff are told, return to previous process).

Explain.voiceover: Here is a simple way to picture it. A hospital does not install a new type of infusion pump on every ward on the same day. It tests it on one ward, trains the staff, and watches closely. If a problem appears, only one ward is affected, and the old pumps are still available.
Explain.stock_query: nurse adjusting infusion pump hospital ward

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see a finished plan. Doctor Ayesha Siddiqui is a public health physician in Pakistan. Her capstone covers a hypothetical tool that flags chest X-rays that may show tuberculosis, for clinician review, in three district clinics.
Demonstrate.stock_query: doctor reviewing chest x-ray in clinic

Demonstrate.voiceover: First, three months of silent mode in one clinic, with results reported by sex, age band, HIV status and X-ray machine. Then a decision point. The governance group starts a pilot only if performance meets an agreed target in every group, and the review workload is acceptable.

slide.title: Ayesha's plan (1)
slide.body: Silent mode, 3 months, one clinic → results by sex, age band, HIV status, X-ray machine → Decision point: target met in every group + acceptable workload → pilot.

Demonstrate.voiceover: The pilot runs for six months in one clinic. Clinicians see the tool's flag only after their own reading, a clinician reads every X-ray, and the tool never clears one alone. Staff get a one-hour training session. A governance group, chaired by the district medical officer and including a community representative, meets monthly.

slide.title: Ayesha's plan (2)
slide.body: Pilot: 6 months, one clinic; flag shown after clinician's own reading; tool never clears an X-ray alone · Training: one hour + short guide · Governance: district medical officer (chair), clinicians, lab lead, DPO, IT, community representative; monthly

Demonstrate.voiceover: She monitors performance against confirmed cases every month, overall and by group, along with overrides and the time from X-ray to test result. She pauses the tool if performance in any group falls below target for two months, if the data feed fails for more than a day, or after any serious incident.

slide.title: Ayesha's plan (3)
slide.body: Monitoring: monthly sensitivity and PPV by group · share of flags overridden · time from X-ray to test result. Stop criteria: below target in any group for 2 months · data feed down > 1 day · any serious incident.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Her recommendation is clear and conditional. Proceed to silent-mode evaluation, and do not use in routine care until the targets are met in every patient group. Remember, stopping a tool safely is a success of governance, not a failure.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a safe plan moves from silent-mode testing to a small pilot, with training, a governance group, monitoring and feedback. Second, monitor performance, equity, use and outcomes, with named people who review the results. Third, write stop criteria and a withdrawal plan before launch, and end your evaluation with a clear recommendation.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Silent mode → pilot, with training, governance, monitoring, feedback. 2. Monitor performance, equity, use, outcomes. 3. Stop criteria and withdrawal plan before launch; clear recommendation.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. This exercise is capstone step three, the last one. You will write your implementation plan, finish your evaluation with a recommendation, and check it against the rubric and the submission checklist. It takes about fifty minutes.

slide.title: Before you submit
slide.body: Key items from the capstone submission checklist: all 10 template sections · intended use names patients, setting, user, decision · figures sourced or labelled synthetic · six risks with owners · silent mode, equity measure, stop criteria, withdrawal plan · no patient data, no clinical advice

CTA.voiceover: Congratulations on completing AI in Healthcare. You can now judge an AI health tool's value, evidence and risks, and plan its safe use, with clinicians always in charge. Submit your capstone evaluation when it is ready. Thank you for learning with us.
